title: Current Density and Drift Velocity
short: I = nqv_dA and J = I/A; electrons drift along at a fraction of a millimeter per second, even though a signal travels nearly at light speed.
trouble: Students think the electrons race through the wire at nearly the speed of light.

blocks.html: Current is charge per second through a wire. Inside a copper wire, what is actually moving, and how fast? The answer is surprising: the electrons creep along far more slowly than a snail, even though the lamp at the end of the wire lights the instant you flip the switch.

$$I = nqv_dA, \qquad J = \frac{I}{A} = nqv_d,$$ where $n$ is the number of free charges per cubic meter, $q$ the charge of each, $v_d$ their average drift velocity and $A$ the wire's cross section. $J$ (A/m²) is the current density.

Picture a cross section of the wire. In a time $\Delta t$, every carrier within a distance $v_d\Delta t$ upstream of it gets through. Those carriers fill a cylinder of volume $Av_d\Delta t$, which holds $nAv_d\Delta t$ of them (a number density, like the charge densities you met earlier). Each carries $q$, so $\Delta Q = nqAv_d\Delta t$, and dividing by $\Delta t$ gives $I = nqv_dA$.

blocks.name: ph-circuit
blocks.cap: Current in a simple circuit. The moving dots show the direction of the current, not the speed of real electrons, which drift far more slowly.

blocks.html: Copper has about one free electron per atom, so $n \approx 8.5 \times 10^{28}\ \text{m}^{-3}$. With so many carriers, a tiny drift carries a large current. The electrons are not sitting still otherwise: they zip about randomly at around $10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$, but in every direction at once, so the random part carries no net charge. The field adds a slow, steady drift on top.

blocks.title: How fast do the electrons drift?
blocks.q: A copper wire of diameter $1.0\ \text{mm}$ carries $2.0\ \text{A}$. Find the drift speed.

blocks.title: A long trip
blocks.q: At that speed, how long does one electron take to travel $1.0\ \text{m}$ along the wire?

blocks.title: Current density and the field inside
blocks.q: In the same wire, find $J$, and the electric field that drives the current (copper's resistivity is about $1.7 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\text{m}$).
steps: Ohm's law, written per unit area and length, is $E = \rho J$: $E = (1.7 \times 10^{-8})(2.55 \times 10^{6}) = 0.0433\ \text{V/m}$.
A field of a few hundredths of a volt per meter is enough. It is not zero, as it would be in electrostatics, because charges are moving and losing energy to the metal.

blocks.html: "The electrons race through the wire at nearly the speed of light." What travels that fast is the field: when you close a switch, the push spreads along the wire in nanoseconds, and electrons everywhere in the circuit, including those already in the lamp, start drifting at once. Each electron creeps along at a fraction of a millimeter per second. Check with the numbers above: at $0.19\ \text{mm/s}$, an electron would take over an hour to cross a room.
